title: The regime and its two questions
paras: Let's start with the regime. Advertisement control runs alongside mainstream planning. The primary Act empowers the Secretary of State to make regulations controlling advertisements, with the two grounds built into that power itself — amenity and public safety, nothing else — and it deems planning permission granted for a compliant display, so sign and structure fall under one regime. The rules are the 2007 regulations, England only, Wales having its own older set; the sections, dates and numbers live in the written guide.

The definition is deliberately vast — any sign, board, notice, device or hoarding, lit or not, used for advertisement, announcement or direction. So a sign that sells nothing is still caught, and an empty frame used for display already counts. The edge is that it must communicate a message: lighting arranged to draw attention to premises is a sign, ordinary or security floodlighting isn't. And there's no de minimis — relief for the trivial comes from the excepted and deemed classes, not the definition.

The drafting is subtractive: everything's defined in, then categories let out again through the schedules — one for what the controls don't touch, one for the classes carrying consent in advance with their conditions. Whatever's left needs express consent. But whichever route it arrives by, you judge on two grounds only, exhaustive and statutory, so straying outside them is unlawful, not just poor practice. Guidance now sits in the Planning Practice Guidance; the old circular's withdrawn but still crops up in stale leaflets.

title: Three doors, not a menu
paras: Three doors, then — not a menu. Every advertisement takes one of three routes: excepted from control altogether, carrying deemed consent granted in advance subject to conditions, or needing express consent by application. And they run in sequence. Excepted? Stop. If not, does it fall within a deemed class and stay inside its limits? Only a display surviving both needs express consent. And keep the two apart: the excepted sign is left alone, the deemed sign let through on terms.

Three exceptions hide traps. Traffic signs: only signs actually authorised under the road traffic legislation are freed — authorisation, not appearance — so an unauthorised roadside board isn't a traffic sign, however official it looks. Enclosed land: ads not readily visible from outside it are excepted, but the test is visibility, not ownership, and a public place reaches well beyond the carriageway to footpaths, bridleways, parks and navigable water. Vehicles: an ad on a vehicle normally used as a moving vehicle is outside control, but a parked trailer used as a billboard is not — it fixes the land as an advertisement site, and swapping in identical trailers changes nothing, because it's the use of the site that counts.

Every exception is bounded, and crossing the limit doesn't shrink it, it extinguishes it — the display becomes an advertisement that was never excepted, and must find a deemed class or apply. Location reshuffles the doors too: in a conservation area, an Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty, a National Park or an Area of Special Control, deemed classes fall away or tighten, so a sign deemed on one high street needs express consent on another. The sign hasn't changed — its setting has.

title: Deemed consent and the everyday classes
paras: Now, deemed consent — the workhorse. The regulations grant consent in advance, in bulk, by class, and most lawful signage never saw an application. Two layers of condition sit on every class. The standard ones run across the scheme: clean, tidy and safe, careful removal in time, and the site owner's permission first — and on the highway that owner is the highway authority, where many otherwise compliant displays fall down. Then each class has its own ceilings on size, height, number, position and illumination, and you've deemed consent only if you satisfy both.

Business premises is the class you'll be asked about most: a business can identify and advertise itself on its own premises, within limits built around the ground-floor fascia. Above that level it's far more restrictive, and illumination tighter than plain signage. The functional classes — identification, direction-to-a-site, forecourt and filling-station signage — are each generous for their purpose, and lost the moment the sign stops identifying or directing and starts advertising to the road. Estate agents' boards run one per property, limited size, on the property, down within fourteen days of completion. And development signage is temporary — contractor boards for the build, marketing signs while units are genuinely unsold — so it can't shelter a 'coming soon' board on a scheme that hasn't started.

Deemed consent ends three ways. Enlarge, raise, multiply or illuminate beyond the class and you step outside it automatically — no bell rings, and the refit that crept a couple of inches taller has left the class whether intended or not. Time-limited classes expire with their event, so the hoarding on a sold-out scheme is out of consent because its time is up. And the authority can deliberately remove deemed consent — a distinct procedural power we'll come to with enforcement.

title: Express consent and the standard conditions
paras: So, express consent. A display lands here either because it never fell within any excepted or deemed class, or because it had a class and left it — on size, height, number, lighting, or a designation that cut the class away. The machinery is the usual one, but the test isn't: it's amenity and public safety alone, and a report weighing need, content, competition or the ordinary run of material considerations won't hold.

The application must describe a known thing — dimensions, position, height, materials, and above all illumination: not lit, externally lit, internally lit, static or changing. Both grounds turn on those particulars, so an advertiser left vague about lighting can install something far brighter than anyone assessed. And the applicant needn't own the land — consent confers no right over it, so a valid consent can still leave the advertiser with no right to erect the sign.

Every express consent carries the standard conditions automatically. You can add bespoke ones, but only in service of the two grounds — limits on illumination, hours, luminance, colour or finish, or removal of an existing sign as the price of the new. Reaching for content — controlling what the advertisement says — is a purpose the power doesn't extend to. For digital displays you condition behaviour, not content: a minimum interval between image changes, no animation, a luminance cap that steps down after dark, and a default to blank or static on malfunction.

Consent runs five years by default, with discretion for shorter or longer. At the end there's no cliff edge: it may carry on, on the same terms, without a fresh application, unless the authority acts through the proper machinery. Change the sign — enlarge, relight, reposition — and it's a new display needing a new application. And the authority may decline a bare repeat: a similar one refused recently, with no significant change since. Declining isn't refusing — it carries no fresh right of appeal.

title: Assessment: what works and what never does
paras: On to assessment. Amenity isn't a property of the sign — it's a relationship between the sign and its setting. You read the setting honestly, then weigh size, proportion to the building, position, height, materials and illumination against it. Express the harm as fit and relationship, not taste. And with illumination you ask twice, because a sign modest by day can dominate by night.

Public safety is narrower and needs harder evidence — overwhelmingly road safety, and it turns on a located hazard, not mere conspicuity, since every advertisement is meant to be noticed. The highway authority's view is central both ways: a case they support is strong, one they won't is in real trouble. And distraction only bites where a demanding location meets a sign that actively holds attention — dense, puzzling, or changing.

Clutter is the harm done by accumulation — no single sign refusable, but the sum a degraded scene — a legitimate amenity ground, judged as the present effect of this sign added to what's there. The trap is refusing on proliferation alone: the 'allow this, must allow others' precedent argument fails, since each future application is judged on its merits; what succeeds is that this sign, in this busy frontage, worsens a harm that's real now. And the excluded arguments fail for one reason — need cuts both ways, since no business case can condemn a harmless sign either, and competition, content and taste simply aren't among the two grounds.

Sensitive settings change the threshold, not the test. In conservation areas, Areas of Outstanding Natural Beauty and National Parks it's still amenity and safety, just against a baseline treated as specially valuable, with deemed classes cut back so more needs express consent. The Area of Special Control goes further — a designation made by the advertisement regime itself, usually rural and often old, within which categories like the hoarding or large freestanding panel are prohibited outright, so no application could succeed. And listed buildings run a parallel consent: advertisement consent doesn't dispense with listed building consent for fixing a sign to one — satisfy one and you've done nothing about the other.

title: Enforcement: the offence, discontinuance and fly-posting
paras: Finally, enforcement. Displaying an advertisement without the consent it needs is a criminal offence, and a continuing one — a fine on conviction, with a further daily sum while it remains. Liability is wide: it reaches whoever's goods, trade or business are advertised, so the authority can pursue the party with the real interest, not just whoever physically put it up — subject to defences of no knowledge, or of reasonable steps taken. Prosecutions are rare all the same, so most enforcement is really the letter that hints at one.

The discontinuance notice reaches where the offence can't — it ends a lawful deemed-consent display. The threshold is deliberately high: it must be necessary to remedy a substantial injury to the amenity of the locality, or a danger to the public, because you're extinguishing an existing lawful right. It works in two stages — served through the proper procedure, with a period before it bites and a right of appeal, it removes the lawfulness, not the sign. Carry on after it takes effect and you've an ordinary unlawful display, and the offence is engaged.

Withdrawal of deemed consent works at the level of the rule, not the display: it removes a class of deemed consent, for a case or across a defined area, so displays of that kind need express consent in future. It isn't prohibition — the application can still be made and granted on merits. Fly-posting and stray highway signs are often better handled outside the regime: the defacement powers remove material without first winning a contest about identity, and a sign on the verge or a lamp column sits on highway land, where powers over unauthorised structures and obstructions are often the fastest route to removal.

The digital, changing-image screen is the sharpest test, and the regime copes because it keys off effect, not technology. You judge it on amenity and safety exactly as a painted board, but it engages both grounds harder — many advertisers on one screen, brightness that transforms the night scene, and a changing image that pulls the eye back, which beside a fast road is the located-hazard point at its sharpest. The control is all in the conditioning: dwell time, no animation, luminance capped and stepped down after dark, failure defaulting to blank. Behaviour, never content.
